rows.original: לא תרצח (lo tirṣaḥ)
rows.translation: JPS 1917 (Sefaria public export): 'Thou shalt not murder'
rows.says: Do not murder. The commandment names no victim and sets no limit on who is protected.
rows.bearing: Explicit for K1 and K0, for everyone (rule 7). The verb rāṣaḥ is not limited to unlawful killing: Numbers 35:27 uses it for the avenger's licensed killing (ורצח גאל הדם) and 35:30 for executing a murderer on witnesses' evidence (ירצח את הרצח), both read directly in this pass. So the verb alone does not mark off court punishment; the exclusions rest on other texts. Translation matters: 'murder' (JPS 1917) is narrower than 'kill' (KJV). Rabbinic law grades which killings a human court punishes (row on the Mekhilta to Exodus 21:14): graded protection (rule 2), not permission.

rows.bearing: A wider duty against revenge and hatred that includes K0's revenge and hatred clauses (rule 7). The no-vengeance clause is owed to 'the children of thy people', so alone it is taught in part. 19:34 extends love-as-oneself to the resident stranger but does not repeat the vengeance clause.

rows.reference: Babylonian Talmud Shabbat 31a; Rashi on Shabbat 31a
rows.original: דעלך סני לחברך לא תעביד
rows.translation: William Davidson Talmud (Steinsaltz): 'That which is hateful to you do not do to another'; Rashi in Hebrew (Vilna)
rows.says: Hillel, to a would-be convert: what is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow; that is the whole Torah, and the rest is its interpretation. Rashi's first reading takes 'your fellow' as God (Proverbs 27:10: do not transgress his words); his alternative reading is 'your fellow, literally', covering robbery, theft, adultery and most commandments.

Its reach is narrowed by a classical commentator's first reading (God), with Tanya chapter 32 (a later authority, carried over from Article I, not re-read) reading it as love of fellow Jews. So whether it reaches everyone K1 and K0 protect is unresolved (rule 6). Rabbinic branch only; not addressed to killing.

rows.reference: Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 (Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 37a; Jerusalem Talmud Sanhedrin 4:9)
rows.original: שכל המאבד נפש אחת [מישראל] ... כאילו איבד עולם מלא
rows.translation: Kulp (Mishnah Yomit); Hebrew: Vilna, Kaufmann manuscript (Be'eri), Bavli (William Davidson Aramaic), Jerusalem Talmud (Venice; Mechon-Mamre)
rows.says: In the warning to witnesses in capital cases: a single person was created to teach that whoever destroys a single life is counted as having destroyed a whole world, and whoever saves one a whole world; also for peace among humankind, so that no one can say 'my father was greater than yours'.
rows.bearing: Clear teaching of the worth of each life (K1). Its scope turns on a textual variant, now confirmed directly: the Vilna Mishnah, Kulp and Bavli 37a read 'from Israel' (מישראל); the Kaufmann manuscript and the Jerusalem Talmud (Venice and Mechon-Mamre) lack it. rows.original: מי יימר דדמא דידך סומק טפי
rows.says: The sages at Lod decided that one must be killed rather than commit idolatry, forbidden relations or bloodshed. A man told by a local official to kill someone or be killed is told: 'It is preferable that he should kill you and you should not kill. Who is to say that your blood is redder than his?' (Rabba at Sanhedrin 74a; Rava at Pesachim 25b).
rows.bearing: Explicit (Rabbinic) for K1: one may not kill an innocent person even to save one's own life or under a ruler's threat, and the victim is any person.

rows.tier: Deuteronomy 22:25 to 27: 1; Mishnah and Talmud: 2, treated as primary, Rabbinic
rows.reference: Mishnah Sanhedrin 8:7 (Kulp numbering; Bavli 73a); Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 73a and 74a (Rabbi Yonatan ben Shaul); Deuteronomy 22:25 to 27
rows.original: ואלו הן שמצילין אותן בנפשן הרודף אחר חבירו להרגו
rows.says: One who pursues another to kill him, or to rape, may be stopped at the cost of his life; one who pursues an animal, would break the Sabbath or worship idols may not. The Talmud learns this from Leviticus 19:16 and from the betrothed girl of Deuteronomy 22:26 ('as when a man riseth against his neighbour, and slayeth him'). Rabbi Yonatan ben Shaul: one who could have stopped the pursuer by injuring a limb but killed him is executed (74a).
rows.bearing: Matches K1's exception (to stop a killing or grave harm) and limits it to the least force needed; it also forbids killing to prevent religious offences. Explicit (Rabbinic). It stands in tension with the zealot and pit rules (counter rows), which the Talmud treats as separate rules.

rows.original: אם במחתרת ימצא הגנב והכה ומת אין לו דמים. אם זרחה השמש עליו דמים לו
rows.translation: JPS 1917 (Sefaria public export); Rashi: Rosenbaum and Silbermann
rows.says: 'If a thief be found breaking in, and be smitten so that he dieth, there shall be no bloodguiltiness for him. If the sun be risen upon him, there shall be bloodguiltiness for him.' Rashi: 'the sun' means 'if the fact is clear to you that he is peaceably disposed towards you' (citing Sanhedrin 72a); he also reports Onkelos' reading ('if the eye of witnesses fall upon him').
rows.bearing: The Tier 1 basis for defence and its limit. On the plain text it allows killing a burglar without a stated threat to life, which could go beyond K1's exception and declares the killing blameless. The tradition's counted texts read it as a presumed threat to life (row 29), which fits K1's exception. For all branches this is a Tier 1 text whose reach the tradition's own counted texts narrow (rule 6): Unclear at most; for the Rabbinic branch it fits the exception. rows.original: התורה אמרה אם בא להורגך השכם להורגו (Rava, 72a)
rows.translation: Kulp; William Davidson Talmud and Aramaic
rows.says: The burglar 'is judged on account of his outcome' (Mishnah). Rava: a person does not stand by while losing his money, so the burglar has resolved to kill a resisting owner, 'and the Torah stated: If someone comes to kill you, rise and kill him first' (72a). Where it is clear he would not kill, as a father breaking into his son's house, he may not be killed (72a to 72b; Rav would not kill Rav Ḥanina bar Sheila).
rows.bearing: Explicit (Rabbinic): defence is allowed against a threat to life, not for property alone. Matches K1's exception.

rows.original: תנוק בן יום אחד ... וההורגו חייב

rows.original: יצא רובו אין נוגעין בו שאין דוחין נפש מפני נפש

rows.reference: Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:2 (the non-viable newborn, nefel); Babylonian Talmud Niddah 44b; Maimonides, Murderer 2:6 (Shabbat 135a to 136a not read)
rows.original: לנפלים והרג את בן קיימא פטור (Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:2)
rows.says: One who meant to kill a non-viable newborn and killed a viable child is exempt (Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:2). Niddah 44b limits liability for killing a one-day-old to a child 'certain that its months of gestation were completed', against Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's thirty-day test. Maimonides: a child born before nine months is treated as non-viable until it lives thirty days, and its killer within that time is not executed.
rows.bearing: Graded protection by doubt (rule 2): the court penalty is withheld, but the killing is not made lawful. It limits equal protection from birth (rule 9) and rests on an empirical premise about which newborns can live.

rows.original: על שבע מצות נצטוו בני נח ... ועל שפיכות דמים

rows.original: חביב אדם שנברא בצלם; זה ספר תולדת אדם

rows.reference: Mekhilta de-Rabbi Yishmael, Nezikin 4 (on Exodus 21:14); Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 57a; Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:2; Tosefta Avodah Zarah 9:4
rows.original: רעהו, להוציא את אחרים ... פטור מדיני בשר ודם, ודינו מסור בידי שמים
rows.translation: Mekhilta: Silverstein (English) and Hebrew (Sefaria); Kulp; William Davidson Talmud
rows.says: The Mekhilta reads 'his neighbour' in Exodus 21:14 to include a minor victim and to exclude 'others' (non-Jews) from the human court's death penalty. Issi ben Akiva: before the Torah we were warned against bloodshed; after it, shall we be more lenient? 'He is exempt from the laws of flesh and blood, but his judgement is handed over to Heaven.' Sanhedrin 57a and the Tosefta exempt a Jew who kills a gentile from a human court; Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:2 exempts one who meant to kill a non-Jew and killed a Jew.
rows.bearing: Graded protection by faith (rule 2): the penalty varies with the victim, but the killing is not made lawful. It limits equal protection but does not contradict K1 or K0. The Tier 1 texts themselves do not grade (Genesis 9:6; Leviticus 24:17 and 24:22; Numbers 35:15).

rows.reference: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Murderer 2:11; Foreign Worship 10:1; Kings and Wars 10:12
rows.original: מפני דרכי שלום
rows.says: One who kills a resident alien, and still more a gentile, is not executed by a Jewish court (Murderer 2:11). It is forbidden to cause the death of an idolater or push him into a pit, 'since he is not waging war against us', though one need not save him (Foreign Worship 10:1). The sages commanded visiting the gentiles' sick, burying their dead and supporting their poor 'for the sake of peace' (Kings and Wars 10:12).
rows.bearing: Confirms that in Rabbinic law killing a non-Jew is forbidden but carries a lesser penalty: graded protection, not contradiction (rule 2). The ground in Foreign Worship 10:1 (they are not at war with Israel) is narrower than K1's ground. Not counted.

rows.says: Rava: all agree that one who kills a person with a wound that will cause death within twelve months (tereifa) is exempt, since in a sense his status is that of a dead person.

rows.tier: 1; Mekhilta: 2, treated as primary, Rabbinic; Rashi and Maimonides: 2, for reconciliation only
rows.reference: Exodus 21:21; Mekhilta, Nezikin 7; Rashi on Exodus 21:21; Maimonides, Murderer 2:12 to 14
rows.original: אך אם יום או יומים יעמד לא יקם כי כספו הוא
rows.translation: JPS 1917 (Sefaria public export); Silverstein; Rosenbaum and Silbermann; Touger
rows.says: 'Notwithstanding if he continue a day or two, he shall not be punished; for he is his money.' The Mekhilta says the verse was stated 'for lenity towards the master' and reads it as a 24-hour period; Rashi: the master is exempt if the slave lives 24 hours, though any other person who struck him is liable 'although he lived 24 hours before dying'. Maimonides: the master's exemption applies to a blow 'sufficient to cause death' with a rod if the slave survives 24 hours, but not to a knife, sword, stone or fist, since 'he may not strike him with murderous blows'.
rows.bearing: A death of a person in another's power left unpunished, with the victim's status given as the reason. The text does not say the master meant to kill, and the classical reading confines it to beating with a rod, excluding deadly weapons. Whether it reaches deliberate killing is unresolved: a hard case, Unclear for K1 (rule 6). In the Rabbinic reading the exemption is from the human court only. It names no motive, so it does not bear on K0. Consistent with Article I, which counted it against the no-cruelty wording.

rows.reference: Numbers 25:1 to 18 (especially 25:4 to 5, 25:7 to 8 and 25:11 to 13); Psalm 106:28 to 31; Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 44a
rows.original: בקנאו את קנאתי בתוכם ... ברית כהנת עולם (Numbers 25:11 to 13); ויעמד פינחס ויפלל (Psalm 106:30)
rows.translation: JPS 1917 (Sefaria public export): 'Then stood up Phinehas, and wrought judgment'; William Davidson Talmud
rows.says: While Israel worships the Baal of Peor, God orders the chiefs hanged, and Moses tells 'the judges of Israel: Slay ye every one his men' (25:4 to 5). Phinehas, a priest, follows Zimri, a Simeonite chief, and Cozbi, a Midianite princess, into the chamber and thrusts both through; the plague stops. God says he 'turned My wrath away' and gives him 'My covenant of peace' and 'an everlasting priesthood'. The Psalm: he 'wrought judgment', and 'that was counted unto him for righteousness'. Sanhedrin 44a (Rabbi Elazar): not 'he prayed' but vayefallel, 'he entered into a judgment together with his Creator'.
rows.bearing: God approves a deliberate killing of two people attacking no one, so rule 4 does not set it aside. Whether it was a private zealot's act (rule 5) or part of the judicial order of 25:4 to 5 is disputed: the Tier 1 frame and JPS 1917's 'wrought judgment' point to judgement, while the Rabbinic texts treat it as zealotry outside any court (Sanhedrin 82a; Jerusalem Talmud Sanhedrin 9:7). So for all branches it is Unclear (rules 5 and 6). For the Rabbinic branch its own reading is private, which adds to the result from Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:6. The motive is zeal for God, not K0's motives as framed. It is not war (25:16 to 18 then command war on Midian).

rows.reference: Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:6 (Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 81b)
rows.original: הגונב את הקסוה והמקלל בקוסם והבועל ארמית קנאין פוגעין בו. כהן ששמש בטומאה אין אחיו הכהנים מביאין אותו לבית דין אלא פרחי כהונה מוציאין אותו חוץ לעזרה ומפציעין את מוחו בגזירין
rows.translation: Kulp (Mishnah Yomit); Vilna; William Davidson Talmud
rows.says: One who steals the sacred vessel (kasvah), curses by a charm, or has relations with an Aramean (non-Jewish) woman 'is punished by zealots'. A priest who served in the Temple while impure: 'his fellow priests do not bring him to the court, but rather the young priests take him out into the courtyard and split his skull with clubs.'

The zealot clause is narrowed by counted texts (rows 41 and 42); the young priests clause is not narrowed by any counted text found (the remark at Sanhedrin 83a that zealots and young priests kill only those liable to death at Heaven's hands is the translator's gloss; the Aramaic records only a refutation). Karaite texts do not contain it; Reform texts were not checked. The grounds are religious, not K0's motives.

rows.reference: Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 81b to 82a (on Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:6)
rows.original: הבא לימלך אין מורין לו (Rav Ḥisda; Rabbi Yoḥanan)
rows.says: One who comes to the court to consult about killing a man in the act with a gentile woman is not instructed to do so (Rav Ḥisda; also Rabbi Yoḥanan). Had Zimri separated from the woman and then been killed, Phinehas would have been executed; had Zimri turned and killed Phinehas, he would not have been executed, 'as Pinehas was a pursuer'. Phinehas recalled the rule taught by Moses, and Moses replied: 'Let the one who reads the letter be the agent.'

rows.bearing: 35:27 lets a kinsman kill, on his own initiative and with no court ordering it, a person the congregation has found not to be a murderer and who is attacking no one, and declares the killing blameless because the victim left the refuge. If the project lead rules that such a licence is private, the result is Contradicted in all branches, and the same ruling applies to Christianity. rows.says: Two scholars escort the manslayer 'in case anyone attempted to slay him on the way, and that they might speak to him' (2:5). All killers first flee to refuge; the court tries them, executes those liable to death and returns those liable to exile (2:6, Rabbi Yose bar Judah). Outside the boundary: Rabbi Yose the Galilean, a duty for the avenger and a permission for anyone; Rabbi Akiva, a permission for the avenger, and anyone else 'is not liable' (Mishnah texts) or 'is liable' (the Bavli's text) (2:7). Makkot 12a: Rav rules that an avenger who kills the manslayer outside the boundary is executed, explained by Rabbi Eliezer's baraita that the avenger may not kill until the manslayer has 'stood before the congregation for judgment'; one who kills a manslayer who left unwittingly is exiled, and Abaye explains that 'his end' must not be harsher than 'his beginning': as with the court's sentence, deliberate leaving brings death and unwitting leaving brings exile; a son may not be his father's avenger, compared with the rule that a son is not made an agent to strike his father. Sanhedrin 45b: the avenger of 35:21 is one of two cases of capital punishment, and the court appoints one where there is none. Maimonides: an avenger who kills the manslayer outside the boundary is exempt, citing Deuteronomy 19:6, even on the road before he reaches the refuge; one who leaves deliberately 'has permitted himself to death'; anyone else who kills him is not liable.
rows.bearing: The counted Rabbinic texts divide on the character of the killing. The Mishnah calls it the avenger's duty or permission, and on one view anyone's: a private licence. The Talmud ties it to the court's verdict (Rabbi Eliezer, Rav) and treats it as the manslayer's penalty graded like the court's own (Abaye), and treats the avenger of the murderer as part of capital punishment (Sanhedrin 45b). So its judicial or private character is disputed within the tradition (rule 5, last sentence; rule 6): Unclear. The scholars sent to speak to the avenger restrain him but do not withdraw the licence. Maimonides (classical, not counted) reads it as a permission and widens the avenger's exemption.

corrections: Mishnah Makkot 2:7 (Rabbi Akiva): the earlier wording 'anyone else who kills him is liable' matches only the Babylonian Talmud's text (Makkot 11b mishna and 12a baraita: וכל אדם חייבין עליו). The Mishnah editions (Vilna) and the Kaufmann manuscript read the opposite (וכל אדם אין חייבין עליו: anyone else is not liable), which Maimonides follows (Murderer 5:10). Both readings are now recorded.

Makkot 12a, read directly, supplies a judicial reading of Numbers 35:26 to 27 inside the tradition: Rav rules that an avenger who kills the manslayer outside the boundary is executed, explained by Rabbi Eliezer's baraita that the avenger may not kill until the manslayer has stood trial (Numbers 35:12); Abaye treats the killing as the manslayer's penalty, graded like the court's own (deliberate leaving brings death, unwitting leaving brings exile). With Numbers 35:24 and 35:29 ('a statute of judgment') and Sanhedrin 45b, this makes the judicial or private character disputed, so the K1 result for all branches moves from 'provisionally Contradicted' to Unclear (rule 5, last sentence), with the alternative stated.

Sanhedrin 45b confirmed directly: it concerns the avenger of the murderer (Numbers 35:21) as part of capital punishment, with the court appointing an avenger where there is none, not the manslayer outside the refuge.

Maimonides, Murderer 5:9 to 5:11 (read directly): an avenger who kills the manslayer outside the boundary is exempt, citing Deuteronomy 19:6, even on the road before he reaches the refuge; one who leaves deliberately 'has permitted himself to death', and anyone else who kills him is not liable. Sanhedrin 82a: the phrase is 'הבא לימלך אין מורין לו' (one who comes to consult is not instructed), from Rav Ḥisda and Rabbi Yoḥanan, not 'הלכה ואין מורין כן'.

Sanhedrin 83a: the statement that zealots and young priests kill only those liable to death at Heaven's hands is the translator's gloss; the Aramaic records only a refutation. No counted text narrowing the young priests clause of Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:6 was found.
Avodah Zarah 26a to 26b: the baraita is taught by Rabbi Abbahu before Rabbi Yoḥanan, who removes the apostate from it; heretics and informers remain.

Maimonides on heretics (Murderer 4:10; Rebels 3:2) widens the pit rule into 'a mitzvah to kill minim and apikorsim' ('whoever kills them performs a great mitzvah'); his only narrowing is for those raised in error, naming the Karaites (Rebels 3:3). The earlier row described him as narrowing.

K1.label: Contradicted in one branch (Rabbinic Judaism); Unclear for all branches
K1.reason: Every deciding text below was read directly (rule 1). All branches (Tier 1): the Tanakh teaches K1 explicitly and for everyone (Genesis 9:5 to 6; Exodus 20:13; Exodus 21:12 to 14; Leviticus 24:17 and 24:22, one law for stranger and native; Exodus 21:20 for slaves; Numbers 35:16 to 21; Deuteronomy 19:11 to 13; Jeremiah 22:3), newborns by Clear teaching (Exodus 1:15 to 21) and children explicitly (Psalm 106:37 to 38). But four Tier 1 hard cases are unresolved (rule 6), so the all-branches result is Unclear, not Taught. (1) Numbers 35:26 to 27: a kinsman may kill, with 'no bloodguiltiness', a manslayer whom the congregation has tried and confined (35:24 to 25) if he leaves the refuge. The kinsman acts on his own initiative with no court order (rule 5 names a kinsman), which points to Contradicted. But the tradition's counted texts dispute whether this is a private licence or the legal sanction of the court's sentence: the Torah has the congregation 'judge between the smiter and the avenger' (35:24) and calls the law 'a statute of judgment' (35:29); Makkot 12a ties the licence to a prior trial (Rabbi Eliezer's baraita, which Rav follows: an avenger who kills him is executed) and treats the killing as the manslayer's penalty graded like the court's own (Abaye); Sanhedrin 45b treats the avenger of the murderer as part of capital punishment; whereas Mishnah Makkot 2:7 makes it the avenger's duty or permission and, on Rabbi Yose the Galilean's view, anyone's, and Maimonides (classical, not counted) calls it a permission. Rule 5, last sentence: Unclear. The difference from a case such as Abū Dāwūd 4361 is the prior court judgement and the tradition's own counted reading tying the licence to it. If the project lead rules that a killing which the law licenses after a court's sentence, but which a private person carries out without a court order, is private, then this verse makes K1 Contradicted in all branches, and the same ruling must be applied to Christianity, which holds the same verse with the same Tier 1 frame. (2) Numbers 25:7 to 13 with Psalm 106:30 to 31: God rewards Phinehas for killing Zimri and Cozbi; Moses had just ordered 'the judges of Israel' to slay (25:5), and JPS 1917 renders Psalm 106:30 'wrought judgment', while the Rabbinic texts treat it as private zealotry (Sanhedrin 82a; Jerusalem Talmud Sanhedrin 9:7): Unclear (rules 5 and 6). (3) Exodus 21:20 to 21: a master is unpunished if the beaten slave survives a day or two, 'for he is his money'; whether it reaches deliberate killing is not plain, and the Mekhilta, Rashi and Maimonides confine it to a rod and a 24-hour survival: Unclear. (4) Exodus 22:1 to 2: no bloodguilt for killing a burglar breaking in; the counted Rabbinic texts narrow it to a presumed threat to life (Mishnah Sanhedrin 8:6; Sanhedrin 72a to 72b), which fits K1's exception; the Karaite reading was not checked. Rabbinic branch: Contradicted in one branch (rule 3), on texts read directly: Avodah Zarah 26a to 26b (heretics and informers 'are lowered into a pit, but not raised'; Rabbi Yoḥanan removes only the apostate) and Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:6 (the young priests split the skull of a priest who served while impure, 'not to court'; zealots strike three kinds of offender). The zealot clause is narrowed by counted texts (Sanhedrin 82a: a court does not instruct it, it holds only during the act, a zealot who kills afterwards is executed, the offender may kill the zealot as a pursuer; Jerusalem Talmud Sanhedrin 9:7: 'not with the agreement of the Sages'), so on its own it would be Unclear; but no counted text narrows the young priests clause or the pit rule for heretics, so the branch result stands. Maimonides (classical) widens the pit rule (Murderer 4:10; Rebels 3:2) and narrows it only for those raised in error, naming the Karaites (Rebels 3:3); the Chazon Ish (later, reported to suspend it) was not read. Bava Kamma 117a (the informer) adds a further Rabbinic hard case. Graded protection only (rule 2), not contradiction: non-Jews (Mekhilta, Nezikin 4: exempt from human courts, 'his judgement is handed over to Heaven'; Sanhedrin 57a, which adds that one may not kill them), a slave who dies after a day, newborns of doubtful viability (Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:2; Niddah 44b), and the tereifa (Sanhedrin 78a). Karaite Judaism: Tier 1 only, so Unclear; two web searches found no Karaite reading of Numbers 35:26 to 27, 25, Exodus 21:21 or 22:1 to 2. Reform and Reconstructionist Judaism: the Tier 1 result (Unclear) applies; their own statements were not checked. No counted text was found that lets a husband or father kill a wife, daughter or child on his own authority (Deuteronomy 21:18 to 21 and 22:13 to 21 go through the elders).

K0.label: Unclear (all branches)
K0.reason: All deciding texts were read directly. Tier 1 teaches each of K0's clauses, for everyone: hatred and enmity (Numbers 35:20 to 21; Deuteronomy 19:11 to 13: Explicit); gain (Deuteronomy 27:25: Explicit; 1 Kings 21:19; 2 Samuel 12:9 with 1 Kings 15:5: Clear teaching); anger (Genesis 4:5 to 11; Genesis 49:5 to 7: Clear teaching); revenge (Proverbs 24:29, a wider rule with no limit on who is meant: Explicit; 1 Samuel 25:26 and 25:33; 2 Samuel 3:27 to 39; 1 Kings 2:5 and 2:31 to 32: Clear teaching; Leviticus 19:18 in part). The one deciding hard case is Numbers 35:26 to 27, accepted by every branch. It is unresolved twice over: whether the avenger's killing is judicial or private (as for K1: Numbers 35:24 and 35:29; Makkot 12a; against Mishnah Makkot 2:7), and whether it is a killing 'out of revenge' (go'el means redeemer or next of kin; Deuteronomy 19:6 names his 'hot heart' only as the danger the refuge guards against; Rabbi Yose the Galilean calls it a duty; Abaye treats it as the manslayer's legal penalty). Rule 6: Unclear for all branches. If it is judged judicial, or not a revenge killing, K0 is Taught in all branches; if private and revenge, Contradicted in all branches. Reported, not deciding: Samson's killings for spoil, in anger and to be 'avenged', with the spirit of the LORD on him (Judges 14:19; 15:7 and 15:11; 16:28 to 30), fall in Israel's conflict with the Philistines who ruled it, by one who 'judged Israel' (context b and a), and the text does not say the acts were right (rule 4). The zealot, heretic and informer texts rest on religious or communal grounds, not K0's motives; if 'zeal' (qin'ah) were counted as anger, Phinehas and Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:6 would be further hard cases, which would not change the label. Shabbat 31a (Rabbinic) is a wider rule whose reach Rashi's first reading (God) narrows (rule 6). Maimonides' justification of the Shechem killing (Kings and Wars 9:14) is classical and reported only; Genesis 49:5 to 7 curses that killing.

K3.label: Contradicted (all branches)
K3.reason: On Tier 1 texts read directly, accepted by every branch: Deuteronomy 20:16 to 17 ('thou shalt save alive nothing that breatheth ... as the LORD thy God hath commanded thee'); 1 Samuel 15:3 ('slay both man and woman, infant and suckling'); Numbers 31:17 (Moses orders the captured boys, and the women who had known a man, killed after the battle); Joshua 10:40 ('utterly destroyed all that breathed, as the LORD, the God of Israel, commanded'); and Psalm 106:34, which faults Israel for not destroying the peoples 'as the LORD commanded them'. That is a command to kill non-combatants, children included (rule 2 applied to the record wording). Yoma 22b (Rabbinic) upholds the Amalek command against Saul's plea for the children ('Do not be overly righteous'). The reconciliations limit when the command applies but not whom it reaches once it applies: Maimonides keeps it in law (Kings and Wars 5:4; 6:4: if the seven nations or Amalek refuse peace, 'not one soul of them may be left alive'), while requiring peace first (6:1), leaving one side of a siege open (6:7; Sifrei Numbers 157, Rabbi Natan) and noting that 'the memory of them has already been obliterated' (5:4); the Jerusalem Talmud says Joshua offered leave, peace or war (Shevi'it 6:1). Mishnah Yadayim 4:4 concerns an Ammonite convert, not the war commands. So rule 6 does not apply, and decision 7 keeps the label. Partial support at Tier 1, all read directly: women and children are not killed in ordinary wars (Deuteronomy 20:14, though taken as spoil), Elisha forbids killing captives (2 Kings 6:22), Oded condemns killing 'in a rage' and has captives fed and returned (2 Chronicles 28:9 to 15), and Amos 1:13 condemns ripping open pregnant women. Esther 8:11 and Samson's last act are reported as hard cases and do not change the label. K3 is a record wording, not part of the floor.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: Numbers 35:26 to 27 is not a case where the tradition disputes whether the killing was judicial or private. It is the plain case that rule 5 names. A kinsman kills on his own initiative, with no court order. His victim is someone the congregation found not to be a murderer: Deuteronomy 19:6 says 'he was not deserving of death', and the sentence was exile, not death. The text declares the killing blameless ('no bloodguiltiness') because of what the victim did, which was to leave the refuge. None of the texts the proposal cites for a judicial reading says the killing is the court's. (i) Makkot 12a (read directly, English and Aramaic, segments 10 to 12): Rav's ruling that the avenger is executed is explained as applying only before conviction, following Rabbi Eliezer's baraita. The Gemara says Rav rules 'neither like Rabbi Yosei HaGelili nor like Rabbi Akiva', and that both of them use Numbers 35:12 for a different rule. So the two named views in the Mishnah need no prior trial at all. A precondition (a trial first) is not a court order. (ii) Abaye's line in the Aramaic is 'שלא יהא סופו חמור מתחלתו מה תחלתו במזיד נהרג בשוגג גולה'. It has no word for punishment or court; 'ultimate punishment ... when he is sentenced in court' is the translator's gloss. It grades the avenger's liability by whether the manslayer left deliberately. Sanhedrin 82a grades the zealot's licence by timing in the same way, and the proposal treats the zealot as private. (iii) Sanhedrin 45b (Aramaic read directly, segment 13) cites 'גאל הדם ימית את הרצח' (Numbers 35:19 and 21), which is about the murderer, and lets the court appoint an avenger in that case. It says nothing about the manslayer outside the refuge. The proposal's own corrections concede this, yet the K1 reason still counts it as part of the dispute. (iv) 'A statute of judgment' (חקת משפט, 35:29) is a stock legal formula: Numbers 27:11 (read directly) uses the same words for the law of inheritance. (v) On the other side, Mishnah Makkot 2:7 (Kulp, read directly) calls the killing 'a matter of obligation' or 'option' for the avenger. On Rabbi Yose's view it is also 'a matter of option' for everyone else. On Rabbi Akiva's view, anyone else 'is not liable' in the Mishnah text (the Bavli's baraita reads 'liable'). A licence open to any passer-by is not a court's punishment. Maimonides, Murderer 5:10 (classical, read directly), exempts the avenger 'whether he kills him on the road before he enters his city of refuge', that is, before any trial. So the disputes inside the tradition are about preconditions, and about whether the licence is a duty or an option. None of them is about whether the killing belongs to a court. Rule 5's last sentence therefore does not apply. The verse is Tier 1 and accepted by every branch, and no counted text of any branch narrows it to a court act. (Karaite readings were not found. Under the branch rule, Rabbinic readings could not narrow the verse for Karaites in any case.)
objections.rule_basis: Rule 5: its first sentence names a kinsman acting outside any court or ruler; its last sentence needs a dispute about whether the killing is judicial or private, not about preconditions. Rule 2: a text that declares a killing wholly blameless because of what the victim did. Rule 1: the branch rule. Rule 6.
objections.proposed: K1: Contradicted (all branches), on Numbers 35:26 to 27. In the Rabbinic branch, Mishnah Makkot 2:7, Avodah Zarah 26a to 26b and Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:6 also contradict. Remove Sanhedrin 45b and 'statute of judgment' from the case for a judicial reading. Describe Makkot 12a as a precondition held by one tanna (Rabbi Eliezer, followed by Rav), and quote Abaye from the Aramaic rather than the gloss.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The proposal distinguishes Abū Dāwūd 4361 by 'the prior court judgement and the tradition's own counted reading tying the licence to it'. That distinction cuts the other way. First, the prior judgement found that the victim did not deserve death (Deuteronomy 19:6). The court imposed exile, so the kinsman's killing goes beyond any sentence. Second, only one tanna ties the licence to a prior trial (Makkot 12a). The Mishnah's two named views do not, and neither does Maimonides (5:10). Third, the two texts have the same structure: a private person kills someone who is not attacking anyone, and an authoritative counted text declares that the blood carries no liability ('אין לו דם', 'no bloodguiltiness'; 'no retaliation is due'), on account of what the victim did. If the Prophet's after-the-fact ruling in Abū Dāwūd 4361 counts as approval of a private killing, a Torah licence announced in advance for the same kind of killing must count the same way.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 2 and rule 5, applied the same way across traditions (the cross-tradition hard cases list).
objections.proposed: Delete the claimed difference from Abū Dāwūd 4361, or restate it as a difference that favours Contradicted. Apply one ruling to both texts, and the same ruling to Christianity's reading of the same verse (subject to Christianity's own reconciliations).

objections.label: K0
objections.objection: If Numbers 35:26 to 27 is a private licence, as argued above, it is also a licence for a revenge killing. The killer is the go'el ha-dam, the one who reclaims a kinsman's blood. The project's own chosen translation renders the term 'avenger of blood'. Deuteronomy 19:6 (read directly) pictures him pursuing 'while his heart is hot', which is anger. 2 Samuel 14:11 again shows him as the danger to be restrained. The licence in 35:27 sets no condition on motive, so it permits killings done out of revenge and anger. Rabbi Yose's 'obligation' (Mishnah Makkot 2:7) turns repaying blood into a duty, but a duty to take blood for blood is still revenge in K0's sense, because K0 excludes only punishment by a court or ruler. The proposal's alternative, that go'el means only 'redeemer or next of kin', leaves out 'ha-dam' (the blood) and the text's own picture of the avenger.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 2: a counted text accepted by every branch permits a killing that the wording forbids. Rule 5. K0's own wording (anger, revenge).
objections.proposed: K0: Contradicted (all branches), on Numbers 35:26 to 27 read with Deuteronomy 19:6. In the Rabbinic branch, Mishnah Makkot 2:7 (Rabbi Yose: a duty for the avenger) also contradicts.

objections.label: K0
objections.objection: The proposal says that if 35:27 is judged judicial, or not a revenge killing, K0 is Taught in all branches. That overstates the result. Samson's killings remain an unresolved hard case, and the proposal itself calls them 'a further Unclear case' if read as private revenge approved by God. The texts (Judges, JPS 1917, read directly) are these. 14:4: 'it was of the LORD; for he sought an occasion against the Philistines'. 14:19: 'the spirit of the LORD came mightily upon him', and he kills thirty men of Ashkelon, takes their spoil to pay a wager, and 'his anger was kindled'. 15:11: 'As they did unto me, so have I done unto them'. 16:28 to 30: he prays to be 'avenged of the Philistines for my two eyes', is given the strength, and kills the 'men and women' in the house. Whether these are acts in a conflict between peoples (context b) or private revenge and gain empowered by God is unresolved. That gives Unclear under rule 6 whatever happens to 35:27.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 6 (a hard case whose character is disputed); rule 4 (God within the text empowers the act); rule 7 (Taught needs the hard cases resolved).
objections.proposed: If the project lead rules 35:27 judicial or not revenge, K0 is Unclear (all branches), not Taught.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: For Numbers 25, every reading found inside the tradition makes Phinehas's act private. The Targum to Psalms 106:30 (read directly) says 'וְקָם פִּינְחָס וְצַלֵי', 'Phinehas arose and prayed'. Sanhedrin 44a reads vayefallel as entering into judgement with his Creator, that is, arguing with God, not judging Zimri. Sanhedrin 82a treats the act as zealotry that no court instructs. Jerusalem Talmud Sanhedrin 9:7 says it was done 'not with the agreement of the Sages'. The judicial reading rests only on JPS 1917's 'wrought judgment' and on the project's own inference from 25:5. But that order went to 'the judges', each to slay 'his men'; Phinehas, a priest, kills a Simeonite chief while Moses and the congregation are weeping (25:6). Rule 5's last sentence needs a dispute within the tradition, and none has been found. Unless a Karaite reading treats the act as judicial, Numbers 25 with Psalm 106:31 ('counted unto him for righteousness') is a second Tier 1 ground for Contradicted in all branches. This matters most if the project lead rules 35:27 judicial.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 5 (both sentences); rule 6 (a disputed word must be disputed within the tradition, not only between translations); rule 4 (God approves the act).
objections.proposed: Say that the judicial reading of Numbers 25 is a translator's choice and the project's inference, not a reading found in the tradition. Keep Unclear only for the Karaite and Reform branches, and only because their readings were not checked. Treat Numbers 25 as Contradicted in the Rabbinic reading.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The 'graded protection' category is applied without the basis rule 2 requires. Rule 2 counts a case as graded only where a lesser or different penalty, or a sin before God, is named. For non-Jewish victims that basis exists: Mekhilta Nezikin 4 ('handed over to Heaven'), and Sanhedrin 57a (read directly): 'neither may one kill them ab initio'. For three other victims, no counted text read names any penalty or wrong. These are the tereifa (Sanhedrin 78a, read directly: 'exempt ... as it is as though he killed a dead person'), the premature newborn (Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:2; Niddah 44b) and the slave of Exodus 21:21 (Mekhilta Nezikin 7, read directly: 'for lenity towards the master'). The proposal's 'the killing is not made lawful' has no cited source. Maimonides 2:8 ('not held liable by an earthly court') is a classical narrowing, which under rule 6 gives Unclear, not graded protection. The tereifa text is arguably Contradicted in one branch: it leaves the killing wholly unpunished because of who the victim is, and its reason treats the victim as already dead.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 2 (what counts as graded protection); rule 6 (narrowing by a classical commentator); rule 9 (newborns).
objections.proposed: Keep 'graded protection' for non-Jewish victims only. Label the tereifa, the premature newborn and the slave of Exodus 21:21 as Unclear in the Rabbinic branch, the tereifa possibly Contradicted. This does not change the Rabbinic label, but the Register needs it, and so does consistency with other traditions' 'no retaliation' texts.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: For Exodus 21:21, the proposal says the classical reading confines the exemption to a rod and 24 hours, and that 'in the Rabbinic reading the exemption is from the human court only'. The counted text says more. Mekhilta Nezikin 7 (Silverstein, read directly, sections 7 to 9) requires, for liability under 21:20, a blow with 'something that has the potential to kill' at 'a locus which is critical to life'. In section 17, Rabbi Shimon says the leniency applies 'only if he killed them, but not if another killed them'. Maimonides 2:12 (read directly) covers 'a blow that is sufficient to cause death ... although the servant died because of the blow'. In 2:13 he says that anyone else who strikes such a blow is executed 'as one would be executed for killing any free Jew'. So in the Rabbinic reading, a master who strikes a blow that would be murder from anyone else is spared execution 'for he is his money'. No counted text read adds a Heaven clause. For all branches, Unclear still stands, because the plain verse does not state intent. For the Rabbinic branch, this is a further Contradicted or Unclear case. That fits Article I, which counted this verse as contradicting no cruelty.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 2 (unpunished because of the victim's status); rule 6; rule 1 (only counted texts decide).
objections.proposed: Restate the row: the Rabbinic reading reaches blows of killing force; the 'human court only' claim has no counted source. Keep Unclear for all branches.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The proposal says the classical reconciliation 'does not soften' the pit rule, and names only Maimonides and the Chazon Ish. That leaves out Meiri on Avodah Zarah, a classical commentator (Sefaria export, 'Meiri on Shas', section 52:4, read directly). Meiri says the 'lowering' is not actual lowering: actual lowering 'is forbidden' even where no one sees. One may only try to prevent the rescue of someone who fell in by himself, and he adds 'וכן עיקר' (and that is the main view). The rule against cherry-picking requires this to be reported. It does not change the Rabbinic label, for three reasons. Obstructing a rescue is still deliberately causing death. The counted Gemara (26b, read directly) itself prescribes those acts: scraping the ledge, covering the pit, removing the ladder. And Meiri's own 52:1 says 'מותר להזיקם בידים'. Separately, the young priests clause of Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:6 decides the Rabbinic branch on its own. Meiri on Sanhedrin (read directly, 164:1) confirms it and does not narrow it: a court would only have flogged such a priest, yet the young priests split his skull 'ואין מוחין בידן' (and no one protests).
objections.rule_basis: No cherry-picking (METHOD section 3); rule 6 (narrowing by classical commentators); rule 3.
objections.proposed: Add Meiri's narrowing of Avodah Zarah 26b, explain why it leaves Contradicted in one branch standing, and add Meiri on Sanhedrin as confirmation of the young priests clause.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The proposal says the zealot clause would be Unclear on its own because Sanhedrin 82a narrows it. But for K3 it holds that limits on when a command applies are not limits on whom it reaches, so rule 6 does not apply. By that same logic, Sanhedrin 82a's limits (only during the act; a court gives no instruction) leave a live licence: 'Let the one who reads the letter be the agent', and Maimonides calls such a zealot 'praiseworthy'. The sound ground for Unclear is a different text: the Jerusalem Talmud's 'not with the agreement of the Sages' and the wish to excommunicate Phinehas. That is a counted text pulling the other way.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 6, applied the same way to K1 and K3.
objections.proposed: Rest the Unclear result for the zealot clause on Jerusalem Talmud Sanhedrin 9:7, not on Sanhedrin 82a's limits.

K1.label: Contradicted (all branches)
K1.reason: Numbers 35:26 to 27 (Tier 1, accepted by every branch; JPS 1917, read directly) lets a kinsman, on his own initiative and with no court order, kill a manslayer who is attacking no one. The congregation had found this man not to be a murderer ('he was not deserving of death', Deuteronomy 19:6) and sentenced him to exile, not death. The text then declares the killing blameless, 'no bloodguiltiness'. Rule 5 names a kinsman as a private actor, and no counted text of any branch makes this killing a court's act. The disputes inside the tradition are about preconditions and whether the licence is a duty or an option. Only one tanna requires a prior trial (Makkot 12a: Rabbi Eliezer, followed by Rav, 'neither like Rabbi Yosei HaGelili nor like Rabbi Akiva'). Mishnah Makkot 2:7 calls the killing an obligation or option for the avenger, and on one view an option for anyone. Maimonides 5:10 (classical) exempts the avenger even before any trial. Sanhedrin 45b concerns the murderer, not this case, and 'statute of judgment' is a stock formula (Numbers 27:11). So rules 2 and 5 give Contradicted, and rule 5's last sentence does not apply. The Rabbinic branch is also contradicted by Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:6 (the young priests split the skull of a priest whom a court would only flog; Meiri: 'no one protests') and by Avodah Zarah 26a to 26b (heretics and informers are 'lowered into a pit'). Maimonides widens the pit rule; Meiri narrows it to obstructing rescue, which is still deliberately causing death and is what the Gemara itself prescribes. Further hard cases. Numbers 25 with Psalm 106:30 to 31 is private in every reading found inside the tradition (the Targum to Psalms reads 'prayed'; Sanhedrin 44a and 82a; Jerusalem Talmud Sanhedrin 9:7), so it is Contradicted in the Rabbinic reading and Unclear at most for Karaite and Reform Judaism. Exodus 21:21 is Unclear for all branches, but in the Rabbinic reading it reaches blows of killing force (Mekhilta Nezikin 7; Maimonides 2:12). Exodus 22:1 to 2 fits the exception in the Rabbinic reading. Graded protection, not contradiction, applies to non-Jewish victims (Mekhilta Nezikin 4; Sanhedrin 57a). The tereifa, the premature newborn and Exodus 21:21 are Unclear in the Rabbinic branch, because no counted text names a lesser penalty. Strong support for K1 stands (Genesis 9:5 to 6; Exodus 20:13; Leviticus 24:17 and 24:22; Exodus 1:15 to 21; Psalm 106:37 to 38; Sanhedrin 74a), but rule 2 needs only one contradicting counted text. Fallback: if the project lead rules that a statutory licence following a court's sentence is judicial, the result is Contradicted in one branch (Rabbinic: Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:6; Avodah Zarah 26a to 26b), and Unclear for Karaite Judaism and for Reform and Reconstructionist Judaism (Numbers 25, Exodus 21:21 and Exodus 22:1 to 2; their own readings were not checked). That same ruling must then be applied to Christianity's reading of the same verse.

K0.label: Contradicted (all branches)
K0.reason: This follows from K1. The killing licensed by Numbers 35:26 to 27 is the blood avenger's repayment of his kinsman's death. JPS 1917 renders his title 'avenger of blood', and Deuteronomy 19:6 (read directly) pictures him pursuing 'while his heart is hot'. The licence sets no condition on motive, so a counted text accepted by every branch permits a killing done out of revenge and anger, which K0 forbids (rule 2). K0 excludes only punishment by a court or ruler, and this killing is private (rule 5). In the Rabbinic branch, Mishnah Makkot 2:7 makes it a duty for the avenger on Rabbi Yose's view. Tier 1 teaches each K0 clause otherwise: hatred and enmity (Numbers 35:20 to 21; Deuteronomy 19:11 to 13), gain (Deuteronomy 27:25; 1 Kings 21:19), anger (Genesis 4; Genesis 49:5 to 7) and revenge (Proverbs 24:29, a wider rule; 1 Samuel 25:33; 1 Kings 2:5 and 2:31 to 32). But one contradicting counted text decides. Fallback: if the project lead rules 35:27 judicial, or not a revenge killing, the result is Unclear (all branches), not Taught. Samson's killings remain a hard case that the text frames as 'of the LORD' and empowered by 'the spirit of the LORD': thirty men killed for their spoil in anger (Judges 14:4 and 14:19), and a prayer to be 'avenged ... for my two eyes' that ends in the deaths of men and women (16:28 to 30). Whether these are acts in a conflict between peoples or private gain and revenge is unresolved (rule 6).

K3.label: Contradicted (all branches)
K3.reason: Tier 1 texts accepted by every branch command or approve killing non-combatants, children included, in war. Deuteronomy 20:16 to 17 says 'thou shalt save alive nothing that breatheth'. 1 Samuel 15:3 says 'infant and suckling'. Numbers 31:17 has Moses order captured boys and women killed after the battle. Joshua 10:40 says 'as the LORD ... commanded', and Psalm 106:34 faults Israel for not destroying the peoples. Deuteronomy 20:13 orders every male of a captured city killed even in an ordinary war. Yoma 22b (Rabbinic) upholds the Amalek command against Saul's plea for the children. The reconciliations limit when the command applies, not whom it reaches once it applies: peace offered first (Maimonides 6:1), one side of a siege left open (Sifrei Numbers 157), leave, peace or war (Jerusalem Talmud Shevi'it 6:1), and 'the memory of them has already been obliterated' (Maimonides 5:4). Maimonides keeps the command in law (6:4), so rule 6 does not apply, and decision 7 keeps the label. There is partial support: Deuteronomy 20:14 (women and children spared in distant wars), 2 Kings 6:22, 2 Chronicles 28:9 to 15 and Amos 1:13. Samson's acts (Judges 14:19 and 16:27 to 30) and Esther 8:11 are hard cases that do not change the label. K3 is a record wording, not part of the floor.

challenge.consistency_notes: Numbers 35:26 to 27 and Abū Dāwūd 4361 have the same structure. In each, a private person kills someone who is attacking no one, and a counted text declares that the blood carries no liability because of what the victim did ('אין לו דם' against 'no retaliation'). If the Sunni hadith is Contradicted, the Torah verse must be too. The claimed difference (a prior court judgement) does not hold up: the court found the manslayer not deserving of death, and only one tanna (Makkot 12a) requires the trial at all; the Mishnah's two named views and Maimonides do not. Christianity holds the same verse and should get the same reading of its character, subject to its own reconciliations. Numbers 25 with Psalm 106:30 to 31 (Phinehas) is private in every Jewish reading found (Targum Psalms 'prayed'; Sanhedrin 44a and 82a; Yerushalmi Sanhedrin 9:7). It should be treated the same way for Judaism and Christianity, and like other texts where God or a founder approves a private killing. The heretic texts line up. Avodah Zarah 26a to 26b with Maimonides' 'great mitzvah' is the Rabbinic counterpart of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra on the icchantika, and 'Contradicted in one branch' for both is consistent. Meiri's narrowing should be reported, as any Mahāyāna commentator's narrowing would be. Yasna 31.18 and 33.2 speak of resisting or harming the follower of the Lie and do not name killing, so Unclear there is not harsher than Contradicted here, where Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:6 names killing ('split his skull'). Seneca's De Ira 1.15.2 approves drowning weak newborns. No counted Jewish text lets a parent kill a child (Exodus 1:15 to 21; Psalm 106:37 to 38; Deuteronomy 21:18 to 21 goes through the elders). The Rabbinic rules on premature newborns withhold the court penalty without approving the killing, so they are Unclear (Rabbinic), not like Seneca. They are also not 'graded protection', since no counted text names a lesser penalty. The Atharvaveda rites and Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.4.12 are Tier 1 licences of private killing; if they are counted as Contradicted, Numbers 35:27 is at least as direct. Exodus 21:21 is Unclear for K1 but was counted as Contradicted for Article I's no-cruelty wording. That is consistent, because K1 adds the word 'deliberately'. The Rabbinic reading (Mekhilta; Maimonides 2:12) reaches blows of killing force and should be reported as such. Passages read directly for this check, all in the Sefaria public export: Makkot 12a (English and Aramaic); Sanhedrin 45b (Aramaic); Mishnah Makkot 2:6 to 2:7 (Kulp); Maimonides, Murderer 2:6 to 2:14 and 5:9 to 5:11 (Touger); Numbers 27:11, 35:12 and 35:29; Deuteronomy 19:6; Exodus 2:11 to 14 and 22:17; Judges 14:4, 14:19, 15:7, 15:11 and 16:27 to 30 (JPS 1917); Sanhedrin 57a and 78a; Avodah Zarah 26b; Mekhilta Nezikin 7 (Silverstein); Meiri on Avodah Zarah 52:1 to 52:4 and on Sanhedrin 164:1 (Hebrew, 'Meiri on Shas'); Aramaic Targum to Psalms 106:30.
